analysis.one_liner: Taxes the unrealized gains of wealthy people who give up US citizenship to escape taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax wealthy expatriates' gains was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat all property of wealthy Americans who renounce their citizenship as if sold the day before they expatriate, taxing the gains then, with a $600,000 exclusion. It would also tax gifts and bequests over $10,000 from expatriates to US residents. It offers deferral only with adequate security and waiver of treaty protections, and exempts certain dual citizens, minors, and retirement accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary US taxpayers, who would no longer effectively subsidize a system where wealthy individuals renounce citizenship to permanently escape tax on large gains. It also preserves money for the Treasury.

how_it_helps.text: Marks all property of covered expatriates to market, taxing the gain the day before expatriation, closing a route by which the very wealthy leave and never pay tax on their gains [S2][S3].
Taxes covered gifts and bequests from expatriates over $10,000 at the estate tax rate, preventing expatriates from leaving large inheritances to US residents untaxed [S2][S3].
Deferral requires adequate security (e.g. a bond) and waiver of treaty rights, so those who put off the tax cannot simply disappear from the IRS's reach [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy US citizens and long-term residents who renounce citizenship or green cards to escape US tax; also their trustees and any US recipients of their large gifts or inheritances.

drawbacks.text: The mark-to-market tax is complex to administer, requires valuation of illiquid assets, and could catch some expatriates with only paper gains and no cash to pay the tax, though a $600,000 gain exclusion, deferral options, and exemptions for dual citizens and minors soften this [S2][S3].

Detractors may view it as a punitive exit tax that discourages lawful renunciation or cross-border life for dual citizens and long-term residents, though the bill's own exceptions aim to limit this [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is closing a large loophole used almost exclusively by the very wealthy to avoid tax on gains. The cost is administrative complexity and some compliance burden for affected expatriates and trustees, mitigated by exclusions and deferral options. On balance it is a targeted, sensible fix rather than a broad burden on ordinary taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced further; the Congress ended before any committee action or floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 30, 2003 by Sen. Harkin, with Sen. Stabenow, and immediately referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S5][S1].
No committee vote, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the action history ends at referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals who renounce US citizenship to avoid tax on gains are better off, since the loophole this bill would have closed remains open. The Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, did not disturb the status quo.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on the record about it

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (108th Congress)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, leaving it without committee or floor action

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats, but the bill drew no recorded opposition votes or statements, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Wealthy individuals considering renouncing US citizenship for tax reasons
industries.note: Would face a mark-to-market exit tax on unrealized gains and a tax on large gifts and bequests to US residents. Their interest in keeping the expatriation loophole runs against ordinary taxpayers who would otherwise bear the shift.

industries.industry: Tax advisors and estate planners serving high-net-worth clients
industries.note: Would face more complex compliance for expatriation and for trusts and bequests involving expatriates. It is a cost to practitioners but reduces a planning opportunity that benefits only the wealthy.
Would collect tax currently avoided by expatriation, reducing the burden on those who stay and pay.
